title: Scaling Dimensions and Two-Point Amplitudes from Operator Covariance Matrices
abstract: The long distance behavior of two-point functions of critical lattice statistical mechanics models depend on detailed information of the underlying quantum field theory. Yet these universal properties can be difficult to extract because generic lattice operators couple to the infinite hierarchy of continuum scaling operators with unknown coefficients. Recently in Physical Review E 114, 024146 (2026), one approach to disentangle some of this information was proposed using the eigen-decomposition of the operator covariance matrix constructed from cross correlations of a finite set of $N_\ell$ lattice operators. In this work we analyze this method in detail. We provide an explicit proof that under the assumption of scale invariance the leading decay of the eigenvalues are controlled by the smallest $N_\ell$ scaling dimensions, even after taking irrelevant perturbations into account. Based on this understanding, we propose a new method by which the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix can be used to construct the amplitudes of the continuum two-point correlation functions. This allows for a complete determination of the structure of the continuum two-point functions from the lattice covariance matrix. We demonstrate our ideas both on synthetic data sets (drawn from the scaling hypothesis) and numerically exact data for the two dimensional Ising model.
summary: This work develops a rigorous method to determine the universal two-point correlation amplitudes of critical lattice models using only the operator covariance matrix. By analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the matrix's eigenvalues and eigenvectors, the authors show that the full structure of the continuum correlation functions can be reconstructed from finite lattice measurements. This provides a powerful, non-perturbative tool for studying critical phenomena.
main_problem: The paper aims to extract universal properties, specifically scaling dimensions and two-point amplitudes, characterizing the long-distance behavior of critical lattice statistical mechanics models.
main_result: The authors provide a method to completely determine the structure of continuum two-point functions solely from the lattice operator covariance matrix by analyzing its asymptotic eigenvalue decay and eigenvectors.
method: The core method involves analyzing the eigen-decomposition of the operator covariance matrix, $C_{ij}(r)$, constructed from cross-correlations of lattice operators, and using scaling-collapse analysis on normalized cross ratios.
model_or_system: The study focuses on critical lattice statistical mechanics models, whose long-distance physics are governed by continuum massless Euclidean quantum field theories, exemplified by the two-dimensional Ising model.
key_observables: Scaling dimensions ($\Delta_a$), two-point amplitudes ($k_{ab}$), and the normalized cross ratio $ho_{ab}(r; R)$.
important_parameters: The separation distance $r$, the reference separation $R$, and the scaling dimensions $\Delta_a$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes scale invariance at the critical point and that the lattice operators can be expanded in terms of continuum scaling operators.
figures_summary: Figures show the eigenvalue spectra of the covariance matrix for different sectors ($	ilde{s}$), and the main results are presented via scaling-collapse plots of the normalized cross ratio $|ho_{12}(r; R)|$ against $r/R$, which match predicted CFT amplitudes.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the covariance matrix eigenvalues. It then details the procedure to reduce the infinite sum to a finite basis and finally uses the normalized cross ratio $ho_{ab}(r; R)$ to extract the two-point amplitudes via scaling collapse.
why_interesting: While focused on critical phenomena, the rigorous mathematical machinery developed for extracting universal amplitudes from finite measurements (the covariance matrix) is highly relevant for analyzing correlation functions in complex quantum systems.
